questions.question_text: A YouTube short video is getting viral according to $f(t)=-2t^{3}+3t^{2}+5$ . At what time does the video get maximum number of shares? ( $t$ is in hours)
questions.question_html: A YouTube short video is getting viral according to $f(t)=-2t^{3}+3t^{2}+5$ . At what time does the video get maximum number of shares? ( $t$ is in hours)
questions.explanation_text: The number of shares is given by $f(t)=-2t^{3}+3t^{2}+5$ To find when the video gets the maximum number of shares, we differentiate $f(t)$ with respect to $t$ . $f^{'}(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(-2t^{3}+3t^{2}+5)$ $f^{'}(t)=-6t^{2}+6t$ For maximum or minimum value, put $f^{'}(t)=0$ $-6t^{2}+6t=0$ $6t(1-t)=0$ So, $t=0\text{or}t=1$ Now check the nature using the second derivative. $f^{''}(t)=-12t+6$ At $t=1$ , $f^{''}(1)=-12(1)+6=-6$ Since this is negative, $f(t)$ has a maximum at $t=1$ So, the video gets the maximum number of shares after $1\text{hour}$ Correct option: Option A.
questions.explanation_html:
The number of shares is given by

$f(t)=-2t^{3}+3t^{2}+5$

To find when the video gets the maximum number of shares, we differentiate $f(t)$ with respect to $t$ .

$f^{'}(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(-2t^{3}+3t^{2}+5)$

$f^{'}(t)=-6t^{2}+6t$

For maximum or minimum value, put

$f^{'}(t)=0$

$-6t^{2}+6t=0$

$6t(1-t)=0$

So,

$t=0\text{or}t=1$

Now check the nature using the second derivative.

$f^{''}(t)=-12t+6$

At $t=1$ ,

$f^{''}(1)=-12(1)+6=-6$

Since this is negative, $f(t)$ has a maximum at

$t=1$

So, the video gets the maximum number of shares after

$1\text{hour}$

Correct option: Option A.

questions.question_text: The distance ' $s$ ' in meters travelled by a particle in ' $t$ ' seconds is given by $s=\frac{2t^{3}}{3}-18t+\frac{5}{3}$ . The acceleration when the particle comes to rest is :
questions.question_html: The distance ' $s$ ' in meters travelled by a particle in ' $t$ ' seconds is given by $s=\frac{2t^{3}}{3}-18t+\frac{5}{3}$ . The acceleration when the particle comes to rest is :
questions.explanation_text: To find the acceleration when the particle comes to rest, we first have to determine at what time ' $t$ ' the particle comes to rest. A particle comes to rest when its velocity is zero. The velocity ' $v$ ' of a particle is given by the derivative of the position function with respect to time, which in this case is $v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$ Let us find the velocity function by differentiating the given position function: $v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}-18t+\frac{5}{3})=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{2t^{3}}{3})-\frac{d}{dt}(18t)+\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{5}{3})$ Applying the differentiation rules, we get: $v(t)=\frac{2}{3} \cdot 3t^{2}-18=2t^{2}-18$ Now, we will set the velocity to zero to find the time ' $t$ ' when the particle comes to rest: $0=v(t)=2t^{2}-18$ Solving for ' $t$ ' gives: $2t^{2}=18$ $t^{2}=\frac{18}{2}$ $t^{2}=9$ $t= \pm 3$ Since time cannot be negative, we consider ' $t=3$ ' seconds. Now we need to find the acceleration at t=3 seconds. Acceleration ' $a$ ' is the derivative of the velocity function, i.e., $a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}$ Let us differentiate the velocity function to find the acceleration function: $a(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(2t^{2}-18)=\frac{d}{dt}(2t^{2})-\frac{d}{dt}(18)$ Applying the differentiation rules, we get: $a(t)=2 \cdot 2t-0=4t$ Finally, we find the acceleration when the particle comes to rest, i.e. at $t=3$ seconds: $a(3)=4 \cdot 3=12m/s^{2}$ Therefore, the acceleration when the particle comes to rest is $12m/s^{2}$ , which corresponds to Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
To find the acceleration when the particle comes to rest, we first have to determine at what time ' $t$ ' the particle comes to rest. A particle comes to rest when its velocity is zero. The velocity ' $v$ ' of a particle is given by the derivative of the position function with respect to time, which in this case is

$v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$

Let us find the velocity function by differentiating the given position function:

$v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}-18t+\frac{5}{3})=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{2t^{3}}{3})-\frac{d}{dt}(18t)+\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{5}{3})$

Applying the differentiation rules, we get:

$v(t)=\frac{2}{3} \cdot 3t^{2}-18=2t^{2}-18$

Now, we will set the velocity to zero to find the time ' $t$ ' when the particle comes to rest:

$0=v(t)=2t^{2}-18$

Solving for ' $t$ ' gives:

$2t^{2}=18$

$t^{2}=\frac{18}{2}$

$t^{2}=9$

$t= \pm 3$

Since time cannot be negative, we consider ' $t=3$ ' seconds.

Now we need to find the acceleration at t=3 seconds. Acceleration ' $a$ ' is the derivative of the velocity function, i.e.,

$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}$

Let us differentiate the velocity function to find the acceleration function:

$a(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(2t^{2}-18)=\frac{d}{dt}(2t^{2})-\frac{d}{dt}(18)$

Applying the differentiation rules, we get:

$a(t)=2 \cdot 2t-0=4t$

Finally, we find the acceleration when the particle comes to rest, i.e. at $t=3$ seconds:

$a(3)=4 \cdot 3=12m/s^{2}$

Therefore, the acceleration when the particle comes to rest is $12m/s^{2}$ , which corresponds to Option B.

questions.explanation_text: Given, $f(x)=4sin^{3}x-6sin^{2}x+12sinx+100$ $\begin{aligned} f^{'}(x) & =12sin^{2}x \cdot cosx-12sinxcosx+12cosx \\ & =12cosx[sin^{2}x-sinx+1] \\ & =12cosx[sin^{2}x+(1-sinx)] \end{aligned}$ We know, $1-sinx \ge 0$ and $sin^{2}x \ge 0$ $\therefore sin^{2}x+1-sinx>0$ Therefore, $f^{'}(x)>0$ , when $cosx>0 \Rightarrow x \in (\frac{-\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ So, $f(x)$ is increasing when $x \in (\frac{-\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ and $f^{'}(x)<0$ , when $cosx<0 \Rightarrow x \in (\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2})$ So, $f(x)$ is decreasing when $x \in (\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2})$ Hence, $f(x)$ is decreasing in $(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi)$ .

questions.question_text: The function $f(x)=log(1+x)-\frac{2x}{2+x}$ is increasing on
questions.question_html: The function $f(x)=log(1+x)-\frac{2x}{2+x}$ is increasing on
questions.explanation_text: Given, $f(x)=log(1+x)-\frac{2x}{2+x}$ Differentiating the function w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{(1+x)}(0+1)-2[\frac{(2+x) \times 1-x(0+1)}{(2+x)^{2}}] \\ & =\frac{1}{1+x}-2[\frac{2+x-x}{(2+x)^{2}}]=\frac{1}{1+x}-\frac{4}{(2+x)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{(2+x)^{2}-4(1+x)}{(1+x)(2+x)^{2}}=\frac{4+x^{2}+4x-4-4x}{(x+1)(x+2)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{x^{2}}{(x+1)(x+2)^{2}}=(\frac{x}{x+2})^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{(x+1)} \end{aligned}$ Sign of $f^{'}(x)$ depends on the sign of $\frac{1}{(x+1)}$ $f^{'}(x)>0$ when $x>-1 \Rightarrow$ increasing $f^{'}(x)<0$ when $x<-1 \Rightarrow$ decreasing Hence, $f(x)$ is increasing on $(-1,\infty)$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $f(x)=log(1+x)-\frac{2x}{2+x}$

Differentiating the function w.r.t. $x$ , we get

$\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{(1+x)}(0+1)-2[\frac{(2+x) \times 1-x(0+1)}{(2+x)^{2}}] \\ & =\frac{1}{1+x}-2[\frac{2+x-x}{(2+x)^{2}}]=\frac{1}{1+x}-\frac{4}{(2+x)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{(2+x)^{2}-4(1+x)}{(1+x)(2+x)^{2}}=\frac{4+x^{2}+4x-4-4x}{(x+1)(x+2)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{x^{2}}{(x+1)(x+2)^{2}}=(\frac{x}{x+2})^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{(x+1)} \end{aligned}$

Sign of $f^{'}(x)$ depends on the sign of $\frac{1}{(x+1)}$

$f^{'}(x)>0$ when $x>-1 \Rightarrow$ increasing

$f^{'}(x)<0$ when $x<-1 \Rightarrow$ decreasing

Hence, $f(x)$ is increasing on $(-1,\infty)$ .

questions.question_html: The coordinates of the point on the $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=6$ at which the tangent is equally inclined to the axes is
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=6$ $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=6$ Differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}$ Since, the tangent is equally inclined to the axes. $\begin{aligned} & \frac{dy}{dx}= \pm 1 \Rightarrow -\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}= \pm 1 \\ \Rightarrow & \sqrt{y}= \pm \sqrt{x} \Rightarrow y=x \end{aligned}$ Therefore, $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=6 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x}+\sqrt{x}=6 \Rightarrow 2\sqrt{x}=6$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \sqrt{x}=3 \Rightarrow x=9 \\ & \therefore x=9\text{and}y=9 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The maximum slope of the curve $y=-x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x-27$ is
questions.explanation_text: $y=-x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x-27$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\frac{dy}{dx}=-3x^{2}+6x+2$ Slope of the curve $=-3x^{2}+6x+2$ Let $m=-3x^{2}+6x+2$ $\therefore \frac{dm}{dx}=-6x+6$ Put $\frac{dm}{dx}=0$ to find the critical points, $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & -6x+6=0 \\ \Rightarrow & x=1 \\ & (\frac{d^{2}m}{dx^{2}})_{x=1}=-6<0 \end{aligned}$ Slope is maximum at $x=1$ The maximum slope, $\begin{aligned} m_{max} & =-3(1)^{2}+6(l)+2 \\ & =-3+6+2=5 \end{aligned}$

$y=-x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x-27$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=-3x^{2}+6x+2$

$\therefore \frac{dm}{dx}=-6x+6$

questions.question_html: If the curves $2x=y^{2}$ and $2xy=K$ intersect perpendicularly, then the value of $K^{2}$ is
questions.explanation_text: Given curves are $2x=y^{2}\text{.... (i)}$ and $2xy=K\text{.... (ii)}$ On solving both Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $x=\frac{K^{2/3}}{2}\text{and}=K^{1/3}$ $\therefore \text{Intersecting point of both curves is}(\frac{K^{2/3}}{2},K^{1/3})$ Now differentiate Eq. (i) w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & 2=2y\frac{dy}{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{y} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Slope of tangent at $(\frac{K^{2/3}}{2},K^{1/3})=\frac{1}{K^{1/3}}$ And differentiate Eq. (ii) w.r.t. $x$ , we get $2(x\frac{dy}{dx}+y)=0 \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-y}{x}$ $\therefore$ Slope of tangent at $(\frac{K^{2/3}}{2},K^{1/3})$ $=\frac{-K^{1/3}}{K^{2/3}/2}=-2K^{-1/3}$ Since, both curves intersect perpendicularly $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{1}{K^{1/3}} \times (-2K^{-1/3})=-1 \\ & \Rightarrow -2K^{-2/3}=-1 \Rightarrow K^{2/3}=2 \Rightarrow K^{2}=8 \end{aligned}$

and $2xy=K\text{.... (ii)}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{1}{K^{1/3}} \times (-2K^{-1/3})=-1 \\ & \Rightarrow -2K^{-2/3}=-1 \Rightarrow K^{2/3}=2 \Rightarrow K^{2}=8 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: $f(x)=x^{x}$ has stationary point at
questions.question_html: $f(x)=x^{x}$ has stationary point at
questions.explanation_text: To find the stationary point of the function $f(x)=x^{x}$ , we begin by expressing it in terms of the exponential function: $f(x)=x^{x}=e^{xlogx}$ Next, we calculate the derivative of $f(x)$ : $f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(e^{xlogx})=e^{xlogx} \cdot (1+logx)$ For a stationary point, the derivative $f^{'}(x)$ must be equal to zero: $e^{xlogx} \cdot (1+logx)=0$ Since $e^{xlogx}$ is always positive and can never be zero, this implies: $1+logx=0$ Solving for $x$ , we find: $logx=-1 \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{e}$ Therefore, the function $f(x)=x^{x}$ has a stationary point at $x=\frac{1}{e}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the stationary point of the function $f(x)=x^{x}$ , we begin by expressing it in terms of the exponential function:

$f(x)=x^{x}=e^{xlogx}$

Next, we calculate the derivative of $f(x)$ :

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(e^{xlogx})=e^{xlogx} \cdot (1+logx)$

For a stationary point, the derivative $f^{'}(x)$ must be equal to zero:

$e^{xlogx} \cdot (1+logx)=0$

Since $e^{xlogx}$ is always positive and can never be zero, this implies:

$1+logx=0$

Solving for $x$ , we find:

$logx=-1 \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{e}$

Therefore, the function $f(x)=x^{x}$ has a stationary point at $x=\frac{1}{e}$ .

questions.question_html: Approximate change in the volume $V$ of a cube of side $x$ metres caused by increasing the side by $3%$ is
questions.explanation_text: The explanation calculates the approximate change in the volume of a cube when its side length is increased by 3%. Volume of a Cube : The volume $V$ of a cube with side length $x$ is given by the formula: $V=x^{3}$ Derivative of the Volume : The rate of change of the volume with respect to the side length $x$ is: $\frac{dV}{dx}=3x^{2}$ Change in Side Length : Since the side length is increased by 3%, the change in $x$ is: $dx=3%\text{of}x=0.03x$ Approximate Change in Volume : The approximate change in the volume, $dV$ , is calculated using the derivative: $dV=(\frac{dV}{dx}) \cdot dx=3x^{2} \cdot 0.03x$ This simplifies to: $dV=0.09x^{3}\text{m}^{3}$ Therefore, the approximate change in the volume of the cube is $0.09x^{3}\text{m}^{3}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The explanation calculates the approximate change in the volume of a cube when its side length is increased by 3%.

Volume of a Cube: The volume $V$ of a cube with side length $x$ is given by the formula:

$V=x^{3}$

Derivative of the Volume: The rate of change of the volume with respect to the side length $x$ is:

$\frac{dV}{dx}=3x^{2}$

Change in Side Length: Since the side length is increased by 3%, the change in $x$ is:

$dx=3%\text{of}x=0.03x$

Approximate Change in Volume: The approximate change in the volume, $dV$ , is calculated using the derivative:

$dV=(\frac{dV}{dx}) \cdot dx=3x^{2} \cdot 0.03x$

This simplifies to:

$dV=0.09x^{3}\text{m}^{3}$

Therefore, the approximate change in the volume of the cube is $0.09x^{3}\text{m}^{3}$ .

questions.question_text: The maximum value of $(\frac{1}{x})^{x}$ is
questions.question_html: The maximum value of $(\frac{1}{x})^{x}$ is
questions.explanation_text: To find the maximum value of the function $f(x)=(\frac{1}{x})^{x}$ , we start by rewriting it in a form that is easier to differentiate: $f(x)=x^{-x}=e^{-xlogx}$ Next, we differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$ : $f^{'}(x)=e^{-xlogx}(-1-logx)$ Simplifying the expression, we have: $f^{'}(x)=-x^{-x}(1+logx)$ To find the critical points for potential maxima or minima, we set $f^{'}(x)=0$ : $-x^{-x}(1+logx)=0$ This implies: $1+logx=0$ Solving for $x$ , we get: $logx=-1 \Rightarrow x=e^{-1}=\frac{1}{e}$ The function $f(x)$ attains a maximum value at this point. Substituting back to find the maximum value: $f(\frac{1}{e})=(\frac{1}{1/e})^{1/e}=e^{1/e}$ Thus, the maximum value of $(\frac{1}{x})^{x}$ is $e^{1/e}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the maximum value of the function $f(x)=(\frac{1}{x})^{x}$ , we start by rewriting it in a form that is easier to differentiate:

$f(x)=x^{-x}=e^{-xlogx}$

Next, we differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$ :

$f^{'}(x)=e^{-xlogx}(-1-logx)$

Simplifying the expression, we have:

$f^{'}(x)=-x^{-x}(1+logx)$

To find the critical points for potential maxima or minima, we set $f^{'}(x)=0$ :

$-x^{-x}(1+logx)=0$

This implies:

$1+logx=0$

Solving for $x$ , we get:

$logx=-1 \Rightarrow x=e^{-1}=\frac{1}{e}$

The function $f(x)$ attains a maximum value at this point. Substituting back to find the maximum value:

$f(\frac{1}{e})=(\frac{1}{1/e})^{1/e}=e^{1/e}$

Thus, the maximum value of $(\frac{1}{x})^{x}$ is $e^{1/e}$ .

questions.question_text: The value of $c$ in mean value theorem for the function $f(x)=x^{2}$ in $[2,4]$ is
questions.question_html: The value of $c$ in mean value theorem for the function $f(x)=x^{2}$ in $[2,4]$ is
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \text{For mean value theorem} \\ & \begin{aligned} & f^{'}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \\ \therefore & f(x)=x^{2} \\ \Rightarrow & f^{'}(x)=2x \\ \therefore & 2c=\frac{f(4)-f(2)}{4-2} \\ \Rightarrow & 2c=\frac{4^{2}-2^{2}}{4-2} \\ \Rightarrow & 2c=4+2 \\ \Rightarrow & 2c=6 \\ \Rightarrow & c=3 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: The function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing in the interval
questions.question_html: The function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing in the interval
questions.explanation_text: To determine where the function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing, we first calculate the derivative of the function: $f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}+2x-5)=2x+2=2(x+1)$ A function is increasing where its derivative is greater than or equal to zero. Thus, we analyze the inequality: $f^{'}(x) \ge 0 \Rightarrow 2(x+1) \ge 0$ Simplifying this inequality, we find: $x+1 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge -1$ Therefore, the function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing on the interval $[-1,\infty)$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine where the function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing, we first calculate the derivative of the function:

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}+2x-5)=2x+2=2(x+1)$

A function is increasing where its derivative is greater than or equal to zero. Thus, we analyze the inequality:

$f^{'}(x) \ge 0 \Rightarrow 2(x+1) \ge 0$

Simplifying this inequality, we find:

$x+1 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge -1$

Therefore, the function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing on the interval $[-1,\infty)$ .

questions.explanation_html:
We have, $y^{2}=x...(i)$

$\begin{aligned} \therefore & 2y\frac{dy}{dx}=1 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2y} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Slope of tangent $=\frac{1}{2y}...(ii)$

Now, tangent makes an angle of $\pi/4$ with $X$ -axis

From Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get

$\frac{1}{2y}=1 \Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{2}$

Putting, $y=\frac{1}{2}$ in Eq. (i), we get

$\begin{aligned} & & (\frac{1}{2})^{2} & =x \\ \Rightarrow & x & =\frac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Required point is $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2})$

questions.question_html: The rate of change of volume of a sphere with respect to its surface area when the radius is 4 cm is
questions.explanation_text: Let the radius of the sphere be a $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \text{Volume,}V=\frac{4}{3}\pi a^{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dV}{da}=\frac{4}{3}\pi(3a^{2})=4\pi a^{2} \end{aligned}$ Again, surface area, $s=4\pi a^{2}$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \frac{ds}{da} & =4\pi(2a)=8\pi a \\ \therefore \frac{dV}{ds} & =\frac{(dV/da)}{(ds/da)} \\ & =\frac{4\pi a^{2}}{8\pi a}=\frac{a}{2}[ \because a=4cm] \\ & =\frac{4}{2} \\ & =2cm^{3}/cm^{2} \end{aligned}$
